title: Die Rübe
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 146. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Noth). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 146 follows a poor ex-soldier whose turnip grows so enormous that he presents it to the king and is rewarded with riches to rival his envious rich brother. The rich brother's attempt to outdo him backfires badly: hired killers bag him up a tree, and a passing student talks him into an even worse trade, a sack of wisdom for a horse. It is one of Grimm's tit-for-tat tales about greed undone by its own cleverness.

sentences.t: Es waren einmal zwei Brüder, die dienten beide als Soldaten, und war der eine reich, der andere arm.
sentences.l: There were once two brothers, those both served as soldiers, and was the one rich, the other poor.
sentences.i: There were once two brothers who both served as soldiers, and the one was rich and the other poor.
sentences.n: The paragraph breaks in this tale are not the 1857 edition’s, which prints it as unbroken prose; they have been put in here to make it easier to follow, and the German is exactly as printed. die dienten is the demonstrative that keeps a spoken sentence moving — “those served” — rather than a relative pronoun. “und war der eine reich” puts the verb first with nothing before it, an older narrative turn English cannot copy.

sentences.t: Da wollte der Arme sich aus seiner Noth helfen, zog den Soldatenrock aus und ward ein Bauer.
sentences.l: Then wanted the poor one to help himself out of his need, pulled the soldier’s coat off and became a farmer.
sentences.i: Then the poor one thought to help himself out of his want; he took off the soldier’s coat and became a farmer.
sentences.n: der Arme is an adjective standing as a noun, the poor one. “sich aus seiner Noth helfen” is to get oneself out of one’s need, and Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not. “den Soldatenrock ausziehen” is to leave the army — the coat stands for the whole service, as the next paragraph makes plain.

sentences.t: Also grub und hackte er sein Stückchen Acker und säte Rübsamen.
sentences.l: So dug and hoed he his little piece of field and sowed turnip-seed.
sentences.i: So he dug and hoed his little patch of field and sowed turnip seed.
sentences.n: also = thus, so, never English “also.” Stückchen is the diminutive of Stück, a little piece — and it measures the whole of his fortune. Acker is ploughland, the worked field itself.

sentences.t: Der Same gieng auf, und es wuchs da eine Rübe, die ward groß und stark und zusehends dicker und wollte gar nicht aufhören zu wachsen,
sentences.l: The seed went up, and there grew a turnip, that one became big and strong and visibly thicker and wanted not at all to leave off growing,
sentences.i: The seed came up, and there grew a turnip that became big and strong and thicker as you watched, and would not leave off growing at all,
sentences.n: aufgehen is what seed does: it comes up. “es wuchs da eine Rübe” uses es as a placeholder so the turnip can arrive at the end of the clause, as English says there grew. zusehends means as one watches, visibly. wollen of a thing is not wanting but tending: it would not stop.

sentences.t: so daß sie eine Fürstin aller Rüben heißen konnte, denn nimmer war so eine gesehen, und wird auch nimmer wieder gesehen werden.
sentences.l: so that it could be called a princess of all turnips, for never was such a one seen, and will also never again be seen.
sentences.i: so that it might be called a princess among all turnips, for such a one was never seen, and never will be seen again.
sentences.n: The turnip is sie because Rübe is feminine; German’s “she” is English’s “it,” and the tale keeps saying sie of it for pages. heißen here is to be called. nimmer is the old strong never. The last clause slips into the future tense and speaks straight to the reader’s own day.

sentences.t: Zuletzt war sie so groß, daß sie allein einen ganzen Wagen anfüllte, und zwei Ochsen daran ziehen mußten,
sentences.l: At the last it was so big that it alone filled a whole wagon, and two oxen had to pull at it,
sentences.i: At last it was so big that it filled a whole wagon by itself, and two oxen had to draw it,
sentences.n: allein here is “by itself, on its own,” not “only.” daran = an das, at it — German gathers a preposition and its pronoun into one word of this kind.

sentences.t: und der Bauer wußte nicht was er damit anfangen sollte und obs sein Glück oder sein Unglück wäre.
sentences.l: and the farmer knew not what he should begin with it and whether it were his fortune or his misfortune.
sentences.i: and the farmer did not know what to make of it, nor whether it was his good luck or his bad.
sentences.n: “etwas mit einer Sache anfangen” = to do anything with a thing, to make something of it. obs is ob es. wäre is subjunctive because the question is his, reported rather than asked aloud.

sentences.t: Endlich dachte er „verkaufst du sie, was wirst du großes dafür bekommen, und willst du sie selber essen, so thun die kleinen Rüben denselben Dienst:
sentences.l: At last thought he “sell you it, what great thing will you get for it, and want you to eat it yourself, so the little turnips do the same service:
sentences.i: At last he thought: “If you sell it, what great sum will you get for it? And if you want to eat it yourself, the small turnips do the same service:
sentences.n: Twice a condition is built by putting the verb first with no wenn — “verkaufst du sie” is if you sell it. He thinks of himself as du, which German does freely. “den Dienst thun” = to serve the purpose; thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: am besten ist, du bringst sie dem König und machst ihm eine Verehrung damit.“
sentences.l: best is, you bring it to the king and make him a gift of honour with it.”
sentences.i: the best thing is to take it to the king and make him a present of honour with it.”
sentences.n: “am besten ist” = the best course is. eine Verehrung is a present given out of respect to someone above you; the noun belongs to verehren, to honour, and there is no English word that does its work.

sentences.t: Also lud er sie auf den Wagen, spannte zwei Ochsen vor, brachte sie an den Hof und schenkte sie dem König.
sentences.l: So loaded he it onto the wagon, harnessed two oxen in front, brought it to the court and made a present of it to the king.
sentences.i: So he loaded it onto the wagon, harnessed two oxen in front, brought it to the court and made a present of it to the king.
sentences.n: vorspannen is to harness in front of a vehicle, with the particle vor left at the end of the clause. schenken is to give as a gift, not merely to hand over — the whole plot turns on the difference.

sentences.t: „Was ist das für ein seltsam Ding?“ sagte der König, „mir ist viel Wunderliches vor die Augen gekommen, aber so ein Ungethüm noch nicht;
sentences.l: “What is that for a strange thing?” said the king, “to me has much curious come before the eyes, but such a monster not yet;
sentences.i: “What kind of a strange thing is this?” said the king. “Much that is curious has come before my eyes, but never such a monster;
sentences.n: “was für ein …” is the German for what kind of a. seltsam stands uninflected before its noun, as older German allows. “mir ist … vor die Augen gekommen” puts the person in the dative: it came before the eyes, to me. Ungethüm is the 1857 spelling of Ungetüm, a monstrous thing.

sentences.t: aus was für Samen mag die gewachsen sein? oder dir geräths allein und du bist ein Glückskind.“
sentences.l: out of what kind of seed may it have grown? or to you it succeeds alone and you are a child of fortune.”
sentences.i: out of what kind of seed can it have grown? Or does it prosper for you alone, and you are a child of fortune.”
sentences.n: mögen here is not permission but conjecture: can it have grown. geräths is geräth es, from gerathen (modern geraten), to turn out well, with the person in the dative — it turns out well for you. allein is “for you alone.”

sentences.t: „Ach nein,“ sagte der Bauer, „ein Glückskind bin ich nicht, ich bin ein armer Soldat,
sentences.l: “Ah no,” said the farmer, “a child of fortune I am not, I am a poor soldier,
sentences.i: “Ah no,” said the farmer, “I am no child of fortune; I am a poor soldier,
sentences.n: The predicate stands first — “ein Glückskind bin ich nicht” — which throws the weight onto it, much as English can say “a child of fortune I am not.”

sentences.t: der, weil er sich nicht mehr nähren konnte, den Soldatenrock an den Nagel hieng und das Land baute.
sentences.l: who, because he could no longer feed himself, hung the soldier’s coat on the nail and tilled the land.
sentences.i: who, because he could no longer keep himself, hung the soldier’s coat on the nail and took to the land.
sentences.n: “etwas an den Nagel hängen” is still the German for giving a trade up — hanging it on the nail; hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing. “das Land bauen” is to till the land, and Bauer, farmer, is the same word as the builder in bauen.

sentences.t: Ich habe noch einen Bruder, der ist reich, und Euch, Herr König, auch wohl bekannt, ich aber, weil ich nichts habe, bin von aller Welt vergessen.“
sentences.l: I have besides a brother, that one is rich, and to you, my lord king, also well known, but I, because I have nothing, am by all the world forgotten.”
sentences.i: I have a brother besides; he is rich, and well known to you too, my lord king; but I, because I have nothing, am forgotten by all the world.”
sentences.n: Euch is capitalised because the farmer addresses the king with the respectful plural, where today one would say Sie; in English it is “you” either way. “von aller Welt vergessen” — in a passive the doer stands with von. reich here is the plain adjective, rich.

sentences.t: Da empfand der König Mitleid mit ihm und sprach „deiner Armuth sollst du überhoben und so von mir beschenkt werden, daß du wohl deinem reichen Bruder gleich kommst.“
sentences.l: Then felt the king pity with him and spoke “of your poverty shall you be relieved and so presented by me, that you may well come up to your rich brother.”
sentences.i: Then the king felt pity for him and said: “You shall be relieved of your poverty, and so presented by me that you may well be your rich brother’s equal.”
sentences.n: überheben governs the genitive — deiner Armuth, of your poverty — and Armuth is the 1857 spelling of Armut. “jemandem gleich kommen” is to come up to someone, to be his match; gleich here is not the everyday “at once.”

sentences.t: Da schenkte er ihm eine Menge Gold, Äcker, Wiesen und Herden, und machte ihn steinreich, so daß des andern Bruders Reichthum gar nicht konnte damit verglichen werden.
sentences.l: Then gave he him a quantity of gold, fields, meadows and herds, and made him stone-rich, so that the other brother’s wealth could not at all be compared with it.
sentences.i: Then he gave him a great deal of gold, fields, meadows and herds, and made him rich as stone, so that the other brother’s wealth could not be compared with it at all.
sentences.n: steinreich piles stein- onto reich as an intensifier, the way English says stone-deaf. Herden are flocks and herds — nothing to do with der Herd, a hearth. “des andern Bruders Reichthum” sets the genitive in front of its noun, the older and more formal order.

sentences.t: Als dieser hörte was sein Bruder mit einer einzigen Rübe erworben hatte, beneidete er ihn und sann hin und her wie er sich auch ein solches Glück zuwenden könnte.
sentences.l: When this one heard what his brother had gained with a single turnip, he envied him and pondered this way and that how he too could turn such a fortune toward himself.
sentences.i: When the other heard what his brother had gained with a single turnip, he envied him, and turned it over this way and that, wondering how he too might draw such a fortune to himself.
sentences.n: dieser, “this one,” points at the nearer of the two men — here the rich brother, who has just been named. “hin und her sinnen” is to turn a thing over in the mind. “sich etwas zuwenden” is to turn something toward oneself, with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Er wollts aber noch viel gescheidter anfangen, nahm Gold und Pferde und brachte sie dem König
sentences.l: But he wanted to begin it much more cleverly, took gold and horses and brought them to the king
sentences.i: But he meant to set about it far more shrewdly: he took gold and horses and brought them to the king,
sentences.n: wollts is wollte es. “es gescheidter anfangen” = to go about it more cleverly; gescheidter is the 1857 spelling of gescheiter, and the comparative is the whole of his mistake.

sentences.t: und meinte nicht anders, der würde ihm ein viel größeres Gegengeschenk machen,
sentences.l: and thought nothing else, that one would make him a much greater return-gift,
sentences.i: and never doubted that the king would make him a far greater gift in return,
sentences.n: “nicht anders meinen” is to think it can be no otherwise, to take a thing for granted. der at the head of the clause is the demonstrative, that one, meaning the king. würde is subjunctive: what he expected, not what happened.

sentences.t: denn hätte sein Bruder so viel für eine Rübe bekommen, was würde es ihm für so schöne Dinge nicht alles tragen.
sentences.l: for had his brother got so much for one turnip, what would such fine things not all bring in for him.
sentences.i: for if his brother had got so much for one turnip, what would such fine things as these not bring him in?
sentences.n: “hätte sein Bruder … bekommen” is another condition made by putting the verb first: if his brother had got. tragen of a gift or a field is to bring in, to yield a return. The sentence is a question in sense and carries a full stop, as the 1857 text often does with a thought reported rather than spoken.

sentences.t: Der König nahm das Geschenk und sagte er wüßte ihm nichts wieder zu geben, das seltener und besser wäre als die große Rübe.
sentences.l: The king took the gift and said he knew nothing to give him back that were rarer and better than the great turnip.
sentences.i: The king took the gift and said he knew of nothing to give him in return that was rarer and better than the great turnip.
sentences.n: wüßte and wäre are subjunctives of reported speech, marking the words as the king’s rather than the teller’s. “wieder geben” is to give back, in return — and the king is scrupulously fair.

sentences.t: Also mußte der Reiche seines Bruders Rübe auf einen Wagen legen und nach Haus fahren lassen.
sentences.l: So had the rich one to lay his brother’s turnip onto a wagon and have it driven home.
sentences.i: So the rich man had to load his brother’s turnip onto a wagon and have it carted home.
sentences.n: der Reiche is again an adjective used as a noun, the rich man, answering der Arme in the opening. “fahren lassen” is lassen with an infinitive: to have a thing driven, not to drive it oneself.

sentences.t: Daheim wußte er nicht an wem er seinen Zorn und Ärger auslassen sollte, bis ihm böse Gedanken kamen und er beschloß seinen Bruder zu tödten.
sentences.l: At home he knew not on whom he should let out his wrath and vexation, until evil thoughts came to him and he resolved to kill his brother.
sentences.i: At home he did not know on whom to vent his wrath and vexation, until evil thoughts came to him and he resolved to kill his brother.
sentences.n: “seinen Zorn an jemandem auslassen” is to vent one’s anger on someone. “ihm kamen böse Gedanken” gives the man the dative: the thoughts came to him, as though from outside — the German does not say he had them. tödten is the 1857 spelling of töten.

sentences.t: Er gewann Mörder, die mußten sich in einen Hinterhalt stellen,
sentences.l: He got murderers, those had to place themselves in an ambush,
sentences.i: He got murderers, and they had to post themselves in ambush,
sentences.n: gewinnen here is not to win but to get, to procure — he found men and bought them. die is once more the demonstrative carrying the sentence on: those had to.

sentences.t: und darauf gieng er zu seinem Bruder und sprach „lieber Bruder, ich weiß einen heimlichen Schatz, den wollen wir mit einander heben und theilen.“
sentences.l: and thereupon went he to his brother and spoke “dear brother, I know a hidden treasure, that one we will raise together and divide.”
sentences.i: and thereupon he went to his brother and said: “Dear brother, I know of a hidden treasure; let us raise it together and divide it.”
sentences.n: “einen Schatz heben” is the set phrase for lifting a buried hoard out of the ground. den at the head of the clause is the demonstrative object, that one, put first for weight. theilen is the 1857 spelling of teilen.

sentences.t: Der andere ließ sichs auch gefallen und gieng ohne Arg mit.
sentences.l: The other let it also please him and went along without guile.
sentences.i: The other agreed to it readily enough and went along suspecting nothing.
sentences.n: “sich etwas gefallen lassen” is to let a thing be done to one, to agree to it — built from gefallen, to please, but no longer meaning it; sichs is sich es. “ohne Arg” is without guile, with no thought of harm — said of the man about to be hanged.

sentences.t: Als sie aber hinauskamen, stürzten die Mörder über ihn her, banden ihn und wollten ihn an einen Baum hängen.
sentences.l: But when they came out, rushed the murderers upon him, bound him and wanted to hang him on a tree.
sentences.i: But when they came out into the open, the murderers rushed upon him, bound him and were going to hang him on a tree.
sentences.n: “über jemanden herstürzen” — the her marks the rush as coming at the victim, from the reader’s side. wollten with an infinitive is often “were about to,” not merely wanted to.

sentences.t: Indem sie eben darüber waren, erscholl aus der Ferne lauter Gesang und Hufschlag,
sentences.l: While they were just about it, there rang out from the distance loud singing and hoofbeats,
sentences.i: Just as they were at it, loud singing and hoofbeats rang out from the distance,
sentences.n: indem here is the older “while, just as,” not the modern “by doing.” “darüber sein” is to be at it, busy with it. lauter is simply laut, loud, with the strong masculine ending to match Gesang — not lauter meaning “nothing but.”

sentences.t: daß ihnen der Schrecken in den Leib fuhr und sie über Hals und Kopf ihren Gefangenen in den Sack steckten, am Ast hinaufwanden und die Flucht ergriffen.
sentences.l: so that the fright shot into their body and they over neck and head stuffed their prisoner into the sack, wound him up on the branch and seized flight.
sentences.i: so that terror shot through them, and head over heels they stuffed their prisoner into the sack, hauled him up onto the branch and took to their heels.
sentences.n: “der Schrecken fuhr ihnen in den Leib” makes the fright the subject and gives the men the dative — it shot into the body, to them. “über Hals und Kopf” is the German for headlong, our head over heels with neck and head reversed. “die Flucht ergreifen” = to take flight.

sentences.t: Er aber arbeitete oben bis er ein Loch im Sack hatte, wodurch er den Kopf stecken konnte.
sentences.l: But he worked away up there until he had a hole in the sack through which he could put the head.
sentences.i: But he worked away up there until he had a hole in the sack through which he could put his head.
sentences.n: arbeiten here is to work away at a thing, to struggle with it. stecken with an object is to put or thrust something somewhere — the same verb the murderers used when they stuffed him in.

sentences.t: Wer aber des Wegs kam, war nichts als ein fahrender Schüler, ein junger Geselle, der fröhlich sein Lied singend durch den Wald auf der Straße daher ritt.
sentences.l: But who came along the way was nothing but a travelling scholar, a young fellow, who cheerfully singing his song rode along through the wood on the road.
sentences.i: But the one who came along the road was nobody but a wandering scholar, a young fellow who came riding along the road through the wood, cheerfully singing his song.
sentences.n: “des Wegs kommen” is an old genitive of the route: to come that way. ein fahrender Schüler is a scholar on the road — the wandering student who went from school to school, half learned and half vagabond, and the tale is trading on that reputation. singend is the present participle, the -ing form, which German uses far more sparingly than English.

sentences.t: Wie der oben nun merkte daß einer unter ihm vorbei gieng, rief er „sei mir gegrüßt, zu guter Stunde.“
sentences.l: When the one above now noticed that someone was going past beneath him, he cried “be greeted by me, at a good hour.”
sentences.i: When the man above noticed that someone was passing beneath him, he called out: “Greetings to you, and at a good hour.”
sentences.n: “der oben” — the one up there; German makes a person out of a bare adverb with nothing but an article. “sei mir gegrüßt” is a formal salutation, be greeted by me, with the greeter in the dative.

sentences.t: Der Schüler guckte sich überall um, wußte nicht, wo die Stimme herschallte, endlich sprach er „wer ruft mir?“
sentences.l: The scholar looked himself all around, knew not where the voice rang from, at last he spoke “who calls me?”
sentences.i: The scholar looked all about him, could not tell where the voice came sounding from, and at last said: “Who calls me?”
sentences.n: “sich umgucken” is reflexive, to look about oneself. herschallen sets her- in front of schallen to give the sound a direction — toward the hearer. rufen takes the dative here, “wer ruft mir,” where modern German would use mich.

sentences.t: Da antwortete es aus dem Wipfel „erhebe deine Augen, ich sitze hier oben im Sack der Weisheit:
sentences.l: Then it answered out of the treetop “lift up your eyes, I sit here above in the sack of wisdom:
sentences.i: Then it answered from the treetop: “Lift up your eyes — I am sitting up here in the sack of wisdom;
sentences.n: es is the impersonal subject: it answered — the voice, not yet a man. “erhebe deine Augen” has a Biblical ring in German as in English, and the whole speech that follows is a parody of learning. German’s plain present, ich sitze, is where English says I am sitting.

sentences.t: in kurzer Zeit habe ich große Dinge gelernt, dagegen sind alle Schulen ein Wind:
sentences.l: in a short time have I learnt great things, against that are all schools a wind:
sentences.i: in a short time I have learnt great things, and against that all the schools are so much wind;
sentences.n: dagegen is “set against that.” “ein Wind sein” is to be nothing at all, a puff of air — and the boast is aimed exactly at the schools this listener is riding between.

sentences.t: um ein Weniges, so werde ich ausgelernt haben, herabsteigen und weiser sein als alle Menschen.
sentences.l: in a little, so shall I have finished learning, climb down and be wiser than all people.
sentences.i: in a very little while I shall have finished my learning, come down, and be wiser than all men.
sentences.n: “um ein Weniges” = in a little while, by a little. auslernen is to finish an apprenticeship — a word from the trades, not the university, which is part of the joke. weiser here is the comparative of weise, wiser, and not der Weise, a wise man.

sentences.t: Ich verstehe die Gestirne und Himmelszeichen, das Wehen aller Winde, den Sand im Meer, Heilung der Krankheit, die Kräfte der Kräuter, Vögel und Steine.
sentences.l: I understand the stars and signs of heaven, the blowing of all winds, the sand in the sea, healing of sickness, the powers of herbs, birds and stones.
sentences.i: I understand the stars and the signs of the heavens, the blowing of every wind, the sand in the sea, the healing of sickness, the powers of herbs and birds and stones.
sentences.n: verstehen with a plain object is to have the mastery of a thing, to know it through. das Wehen is an infinitive turned into a noun, the blowing — German makes such nouns from any verb. The catalogue is what a wise man was supposed to command, and it is meant to sound like the contents page of a learned book.

sentences.t: Wärst du einmal darin, du würdest fühlen was für Herrlichkeit aus dem Sack der Weisheit fließt.“
sentences.l: Were you once inside, you would feel what a splendour flows out of the sack of wisdom.”
sentences.i: If you were once inside, you would feel what splendour flows out of the sack of wisdom.”
sentences.n: Another condition made by putting the verb first: wärst du = if you were. “was für Herrlichkeit” = what kind of splendour. The whole pitch is aimed at a young scholar’s vanity, and it lands.

sentences.t: Der Schüler, wie er das alles hörte, erstaunte und sprach „gesegnet sei die Stunde, wo ich dich gefunden habe, könnt ich nicht auch ein wenig in den Sack kommen?“
sentences.l: The scholar, when he heard all that, was astonished and spoke “blessed be the hour where I have found you, could I not also come a little into the sack?”
sentences.i: The scholar, hearing all this, was astonished, and said: “Blessed be the hour in which I found you — might I not come into the sack a little too?”
sentences.n: “gesegnet sei” is the old subjunctive of wishing, blessed be. wo for “in which” of a time is common in these tales where modern German writes in der. könnt is könnte with its ending clipped, which makes the request polite rather than blunt.

sentences.t: Oben der antwortete, als thät ers nicht gerne, „eine kleine Weile will ich dich wohl hinein lassen für Lohn und gute Worte,
sentences.l: Above the one answered, as if he did it not gladly, “a little while I will indeed let you inside for payment and good words,
sentences.i: The one above answered, as though he did it unwillingly: “For a little while I will let you in, for a payment and a civil word,
sentences.n: “Oben der” puts the adverb first and the article after it — the one up there — a thoroughly spoken word order. thät is the old short subjunctive of thun (modern täte), which builds the as-if clause. “für Lohn und gute Worte” is a fixed pair: for money and fair speaking.

sentences.t: aber du mußt doch noch eine Stunde warten, es ist ein Stück übrig, das ich erst lernen muß.“
sentences.l: but you must yet wait an hour still, there is a piece left over that I must first learn.”
sentences.i: but you must wait an hour yet; there is one piece left that I have still to learn.”
sentences.n: doch and noch together press the delay home: but you must wait, all the same. ein Stück is a piece of the curriculum, a lesson still to be got through — the swindle keeps the vocabulary of apprenticeship throughout.

sentences.t: Als der Schüler ein wenig gewartet hatte, war ihm die Zeit zu lang und er bat daß er doch möchte hineingelassen werden, sein Durst nach Weisheit wäre gar zu groß.
sentences.l: When the scholar had waited a little, the time was too long for him and he begged that he might yet be let inside, his thirst after wisdom were far too great.
sentences.i: When the scholar had waited a little the time hung heavy on him, and he begged to be let inside after all, saying his thirst for wisdom was far too great.
sentences.n: “die Zeit wurde ihm lang” is the German for time hanging heavy, with the person in the dative. möchte is subjunctive in the reported request, and wäre keeps the last clause as his own words, though the daß has been dropped.

sentences.t: Da stellte sich der oben als gäbe er endlich nach und sprach „damit ich aus dem Haus der Weisheit heraus kann, mußt du den Sack am Strick herunterlassen, so sollst du eingehen.“
sentences.l: Then the one above made as though he gave in at last and spoke “so that I can get out of the house of wisdom, you must let the sack down on the rope, then shall you go in.”
sentences.i: Then the one above made as though he were giving in at last, and said: “So that I can get out of the house of wisdom, you must let the sack down by the rope, and then you shall go in.”
sentences.n: “sich stellen als …” is to pretend, to make as if, and gäbe … nach is the subjunctive of nachgeben, to give in, with its particle at the end. The sack has quietly become a house — the swindle is in the vocabulary before it is in the deed. “heraus können” leaves the verb of motion out altogether: to be able to get out.

sentences.t: Also ließ der Schüler ihn herunter, band den Sack auf und befreite ihn,
sentences.l: So let the scholar him down, tied the sack open and freed him,
sentences.i: So the scholar let him down, untied the sack and set him free,
sentences.n: “ließ ihn herunter” is herunterlassen pulled apart around its object. aufbinden is to undo what was tied — the particle auf undoes, as it does in aufmachen, to open.

sentences.t: dann rief er selber „nun zieh mich recht geschwind hinauf,“ und wollt geradstehend in den Sack einschreiten.
sentences.l: then cried he himself “now pull me right quickly up,” and wanted standing upright to step into the sack.
sentences.i: then he called out himself: “Now pull me up, and quickly,” and made to step into the sack standing upright.
sentences.n: zieh is the imperative of ziehen with its -e dropped, and hinauf is its particle, sent to the end. recht here strengthens what follows: right quickly. He means to go in upright and feet first, which is the detail the next line turns on.

sentences.t: „Halt!“ sagte der andere, „so gehts nicht an,“ packte ihn beim Kopf, steckte ihn umgekehrt in den Sack, schnürte zu,
sentences.l: “Stop!” said the other, “that way it does not do,” seized him by the head, put him the other way up into the sack, laced it shut,
sentences.i: “Stop!” said the other. “That is not how it is done” — and seized him by the head, thrust him into the sack head downwards, laced it shut,
sentences.n: “es geht nicht an” = it will not do, it is not allowed; gehts is geht es. “beim Kopf packen” takes bei where English takes by. umgekehrt is the past participle of umkehren serving as an adverb: turned round, upside down. zuschnüren, to lace shut, leaves its zu at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: und zog den Jünger der Weisheit am Strick baumwärts, dann schwengelte er ihn in der Luft und sprach „wie stehts, mein lieber Geselle?
sentences.l: and pulled the disciple of wisdom on the rope treewards, then he swung him in the air and spoke “how stands it, my dear fellow?
sentences.i: and hauled the disciple of wisdom up the tree by the rope; then he swung him about in the air and said: “How goes it, my dear fellow?
sentences.n: der Jünger is a disciple, a follower — the word used of the disciples in the German Bible, and not the comparative of jung, young. baumwärts is built with the old ending -wärts, in the direction of: treewards. “wie stehts?” = how do things stand, how goes it.

sentences.t: siehe, schon fühlst du daß dir die Weisheit kommt und machst gute Erfahrung, sitze also fein ruhig, bis du klüger wirst.“
sentences.l: behold, already you feel that wisdom comes to you and make good experience, so sit nicely quiet until you become cleverer.”
sentences.i: See, you feel already that wisdom is coming to you and that you are profiting by it; so sit quite still until you grow wiser.”
sentences.n: siehe is the old imperative of sehen, pointing at what comes next. “dir kommt die Weisheit” has the dative again: wisdom comes to you. “gute Erfahrung machen” is to come off well by a thing. sitze keeps its full imperative -e and sounds formal beside the mockery.

sentences.t: Damit stieg er auf des Schülers Pferd, ritt fort, schickte aber nach einer Stunde jemand, der ihn wieder herablassen mußte.
sentences.l: With that mounted he the scholar’s horse, rode away, but sent after an hour someone who had to let him down again.
sentences.i: With that he mounted the scholar’s horse and rode off; but after an hour he sent somebody who had to let him down again.
sentences.n: damit is “with that, thereupon.” “des Schülers Pferd” again sets the genitive in front of its noun. The tale ends on that single act of mercy — the scholar hangs exactly one hour — and says no more about either brother.

glossary.arg: Arg — guile, ill intent (the noun in “ohne Arg”, without guile; the adjective arg means bad, grievous)
glossary.arm: arm — poor (adjective; der Arme, the poor man; the noun der Arm means an arm)
glossary.band: aufbinden — untied, undid (3rd sg. past with separable auf-: ‘band den Sack auf’; the noun das Band means a band, a ribbon)
glossary.baute: bauen — tilled, cultivated (3rd sg. past; das Land bauen, to till the land; bauen otherwise means to build)
glossary.dicker: dick — thicker (comparative of dick, thick, fat)
glossary.dinge: das Ding — thing (pl. Dinge; the phrase guter Dinge sein, to be in good spirits, is a separate idiom)
glossary.eingehen: eingehen — to go in, to enter (infinitive; separable ein-)
glossary.gefallen: sich etwas gefallen lassen — to agree to a thing, to let it be done to one (infinitive; gefallen alone = to please, and it is also the past participle of fallen)
glossary.gewann: gewinnen — got, procured (3rd sg. past; ‘er gewann Mörder’, he got men to do a murder; also to win, to gain)
glossary.gleich: gleich — equal, a match for (‘jemandem gleich kommen’ = to come up to someone); the same word also means at once, straight away
glossary.guter: gut — good (fem. dat. inflected; zu guter Stunde, at a good hour)
glossary.heißen: heißen — to be called, to be named (infinitive; the same verb also means to bid, to order)
glossary.herablassen: herablassen — to let down, to lower (infinitive; separable herab-)
glossary.jünger: der Jünger — disciple, follower (‘der Jünger der Weisheit’, the disciple of wisdom; not the comparative of jung)
glossary.lauter: laut — loud (adj., masc. nom.; lauter Gesang, loud singing — not lauter meaning “nothing but”)
glossary.pferde: das Pferd — horses (pl.; the same form is also the older dative sg., dem Pferde)
glossary.reich: reich — rich (adjective); also das Reich — kingdom, realm (noun)
glossary.reiche: reich — the rich one, the rich man (adjective used as a noun, der Reiche; the verb reichen means to hand, to reach)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldiers (pl.; ‘als Soldaten dienen’, to serve as soldiers)
glossary.spannte: spannen — harnessed (3rd sg. past; here vorspannen, ‘spannte zwei Ochsen vor’, harnessed two oxen in front)
glossary.stecken: stecken — to put, to stick (something somewhere); also to be stuck, to be lodged in something
glossary.tragen: tragen — to carry; also to bring in, to yield (a return), and to wear (die Krone tragen)
glossary.verglichen: vergleichen — compared (past participle; ‘damit verglichen werden’, to be compared with it)
glossary.weiser: weise — wiser (comparative of the adjective weise; not the noun der Weise, a wise man)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. present; the same spelling is also weiß, white)
